title: Teaching by Asking
paragraphs: Socrates, who lived in Athens in the fifth century BCE, never wrote a book. Much of what we know about him comes from the dialogues of his student Plato, in which he appears walking around the city and talking to anyone willing to answer. His favourite activity was not giving lectures but asking questions.

A typical conversation began when someone claimed to know what a word such as courage or justice meant. Socrates would ask for a definition, then raise examples that did not fit it. Step by step, the speaker was led to see that his confident answer contradicted his other beliefs. According to Plato, Socrates said that his own wisdom lay in recognising how little he knew, while others believed they knew things they did not.

Not everyone enjoyed being questioned in public. In 399 BCE, Socrates was put on trial, accused of failing to honour the city's gods and corrupting young people, and he was sentenced to death. Yet his approach survived him. Today, teachers in law schools and classrooms use a similar method, asking careful questions that help students examine their own reasoning instead of simply memorising answers.

sources.claim: Sokrates MÖ 5. yüzyılda Atina'da yaşadı, hiçbir şey yazmadı; onun hakkında bildiklerimizin büyük kısmı başta öğrencisi Platon'un diyaloglarından gelir.

Sokrates cesaret, adalet gibi kavramların tanımını sorup karşı örneklerle muhatabının inançları arasındaki çelişkiyi gösterirdi; Platon'a göre kendi bilgeliğini ne kadar az bildiğinin farkında olmasında görürdü.
MÖ 399'da Sokrates şehrin tanrılarını tanımamak (dinsizlik) ve gençleri yozlaştırmakla suçlanarak yargılandı ve ölüme mahkum edildi.
Hukuk fakülteleri ders zamanının önemli bölümünü Sokratik diyaloğa ayırır; Sokratik sorgulama hukuk eğitiminde bugün de kullanılan bir yöntemdir.
sources.source: Minnesota Law Review, Dethroning Langdell (Beth Hirschfelder Wilensky); https://scholarship.law.umn.edu/minnlrev/vol107/iss6/8/
